nodes.label: Nation-state Author
nodes.notes: Operation Olympic Games (publicly attributed). Objective: sabotage enrichment without overt kinetic action.

nodes.label: Stuxnet
nodes.notes: ~500KB worm. Four zero-days, two stolen code-signing certs, first known PLC rootkit.

nodes.label: Contractor Laptop
nodes.notes: Patient zero on the IT side — vendor/contractor machine.

nodes.label: Engineering PC
nodes.notes: Windows host. Spreads via USB autorun, network shares, print-spooler flaw (MS10-061).

nodes.label: WinCC SCADA DB
nodes.notes: Siemens WinCC with hard-coded default DB credentials — a propagation vector.

nodes.label: STEP7 / WinCC Eng. WS
nodes.notes: Siemens engineering station. Infects STEP7 projects and hijacks s7otbxdx.dll to intercept PLC comms.

nodes.label: Siemens S7-300 PLC
nodes.notes: Rogue ladder logic injected. First-ever PLC rootkit hides its own code from the engineer.

nodes.label: IR-1 Centrifuge Cascade
nodes.notes: Rotor speed driven out of tolerance (~1064 Hz → 1410 Hz, then 2 Hz). Cumulative damage over months.

nodes.label: Operator HMI / SCADA
nodes.notes: Operators shown pre-recorded 'all normal' values — the sabotage is masked in real time.

nodes.label: Insider courier
nodes.notes: Reported (2019 investigation) to be an engineer recruited by Dutch intelligence who physically introduced Stuxnet on removable media. Earlier theory: unwitting contractors. Either way a human had to cross the air gap.

nodes.label: Global spread · AV discovery 2010
nodes.notes: An aggressive 2010 variant spread beyond Natanz once an infected laptop reconnected to the internet. VirusBlokAda then Symantec analysed it mid-2010 — the first cyber-physical weapon became public.

edges.label: infected laptop taken out, plugged in online

steps.note: Stuxnet (2010) — a nation-state builds the first cyber-physical weapon: four zero-days, stolen code-signing certs, and the first-ever PLC rootkit.
It seeds contractor IT networks. The worm spreads laptop-to-PC via USB autorun, network shares and the print-spooler flaw (MS10-061), and abuses default WinCC database credentials.
The target is air-gapped — no network path in. A human courier carries an infected USB across the gap and into the enrichment facility. This is the only way in.
Inside, Stuxnet rewrites the Siemens S7-300 PLC: it drives centrifuge rotor speeds out of tolerance to wreck them — while replaying pre-recorded 'all normal' values so operators see nothing wrong.
It escaped by accident: an infected laptop later reconnected to the internet, and the aggressive 2010 variant self-propagated worldwide — which is how researchers discovered it.
The full chain: design → IT foothold → human-carried USB across the air gap → physical sabotage of centrifuges → accidental release into the wild.
